Lotto's squandered millions

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate an illusive Pretoria based lawyer and find out how he managed to receive millions from the National Lotteries Commission for supposed charitable projects that never materialised.

Unique Selling Point:
Attorney, Lesley Ramulifh, allegedly received a total of R27.5 million rand from the NLC to refurbish an existing NPO and drug rehabilitation centre in Pretoria. But soon after construction started, the owner of the rehab, Ado Krige, started questioning Lesley on construction delays etc, as well as the fact that contrary to their agreement Lesley wanted Ado to sell the rehab to him. Since then construction (according to an independent report the value of work done only totals R4 million) has stopped. Ado has taken his case to the NLC who seem unwilling to do anything about the situation. Lesley received the R27.5 million by calling himself a director of an NPO called Denzhe Primary Care. We can prove that at least some of the money Denzhe received, about half a million rand, went towards purchasing two Ocean Basket franchises. We can also prove that the construction company Lesley appointed to do the R15 million refurbishment of the rehab, Upbrand Properties was registered in January 2016 with Johannes Kgomotso Letwaba, the older brother of the NLC’s COO, Phillemon Letwaba, as the sole director.

Summary:
Except for the Denzhe deal, we can also link Lesley to 3 other NPO's, Zibsifusion, I am made 4 God's glory, and Dinosys, which received R31 million from the NLC, for projects that don't seem to have materialised. Lesley is the chairperson of I am made 4 God's Glory, while the other two are chaired by people who work for Lesley's law firm Ramulifho Inc.

Further information:
Although the Denzhe story has been reported by Ground Up and then covered in the Citizen, the story has received very little traction.
We have documentary proof of all the funds received and grant allocations made to Ramulifho and his associates.
It is plain to see at Ado's rehab that the work, according to the grant allocation, has not been done.
There is a clear conflict of interest in the NLC's COO and the sole director of the construction company.
The only images we have available of Ramulifho is about 25 instagram posts by his girlfriend Melanie, which show the couple's jetsetting lifestyle in the past two years with trips to Bali, Isreal, Qatar etc and flying first class.
We have internal NLC docs showing the funding of R27.5 mil was approved and paid, and that the NLC did a final site visit to declare the project was completed according to spec. (We cannot show these because source would be compromised).

While Ramulifho needs to answer the allegations against him, the real problem is the NLC releasing funds to him without any sort of due diligence. The NLC needs to be held to account, but in the articles published they have seemed to come off lightly.

Ado Krige

Press Release:


Missing Lottery Millions
With a limited annual budget of about R1,4 billion to support deserving charities around the country – and demand outstripping supply – the National Lotteries Commission is in the spotlight as Carte Blanche investigates how a R27,5-milion grant to a Pretoria-based drug rehabilitation centre was spent. Following allegations that the NPO has little to show for the money invested in its upgrade, we unravel the bookkeeping smoke and mirrors.
Producer: Graham Coetzer
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender


Script:


Lotto Fraud
FINAL
13 April 2019

Voice
Every week, hundreds of thousands of South Africans fork out their hard-earned cash for the chance to become overnight millionaires in games of chance like the Lotto and Powerball. And it’s all for the greater good, since 27% of the roughly R1.4 billion in annual turnover should go to charitable causes.

Link Devi
The National Lotteries Commission, or the NLC, oversees how Lotto funds are distributed to charities and NPO’s around the country. They say they have strict measures in place to control how monies are disbursed. But the process is not always smooth.

Voice
Ado Krige runs a faith-based drug rehabilitation centre in Pretoria called House Regeneration. As a young man he got involved in drugs, but after a run-in with the law, he says he found God and made it his life mission to help others overcome their addictions.

Sound Up Ado
We are into changing people’s lives. Any form of addiction, any destructive habit, has a source, a root in the persons heart. That if you don’t deal with the root issue, they are going to find it very very difficult to break that habit.

Voice
Krige says House Regeneration was a successful enterprise. He never wanted or needed to apply for NLC funding. But in September 2016 he says he was approached by this man, Pretoria based lawyer Lesley Ramulifho. Krige says Ramulifho offered to upgrade and refurbish the rehab via an NLC grant. It looked good on paper, but he was skeptical about the project ever getting off the ground.

Sound Up
The plan was that they were going to spend initially R17 million, which I was very doubtful about, and it would be a synergy of them supplying the funds, we are supplying the know how the knowledge and the therapy and running the program with them side by side.

Voice
These documents, from a source who wants to remain anonymous, show that Lesley Ramulifho applied for and was granted a total of R27.5 million for the rehab project under a non-profit organisation called Denzhe Primary Care.

Sound Up Ado
Both my wife and I thought that this is never going to materialise, I got the fright of my life when my son sent me a whatsapp photograph of bulldozers on site pulling the old buildings down.

Voice
Pleasantly surprised, Krige looked forward to the new facilities, which would include a brand-new auditorium and a state-of-the-art sports centre at a budget of R5 million. But soon after construction started, there were problems.

Sound Up Ado
Ado: Then I also said to him there are no plans, where are the plans going to come from, who’s going to submit the plans?

Devi: Wait, wait, wait….

Ado: He said I’ll take care of that over a long lunch don’t worry about that.

Devi: Wait, wait. There were no plans?

Ado: No Plans.

Devi: But they were already breaking ground here?

Ado: Ja, ja ja.

Devi: But no plans?

Ado: No plans.

Voice:
Over the following months, Krige says disputes between himself and Ramulifho about construction issues and how the money was being spent led to a total breakdown in the relationship between Denzhe and House Regeneration. Denzhe has taken Krige to court and the case verifies many of our leaked records that are now in the public domain. Krige in turn has laid criminal charges against Ramulifho.

Sound Up Ado
As a citizen of this country I have to report corruption, which I did. And it took me eight months before I could get a case number because nobody wanted to take the case.

Sound Up Ado
Ado: Now lo and behold, R5 million standing there.

Devi: What’s that?

Ado: That’s a sport centre.

Devi: No man.

Ado: Ja that’s a sport Centre, R5million rand sports Centre. All that he did there was put on a new roof.

Voice
And he says what currently passes for the sports centre was an existing building that used to be his lapa.

Sound Up Ado
This was our table; you can see it’s old. Ok, this used to be my Lapa and the equipment that you see in here I promise you is all my old equipment.

Voice
According to Krige the building shown as the sports centre in the architectural drawings does in fact not exist on site,

Link Devi
I need your help here. I need you to use your imagination and picture a R5 million sports Centre, right here, with all the bells and whistles. Can you picture it? Neither can I.

Voice
A new classroom, two blocks of living quarters and the auditorium have been finished but Krige says they’re shoddily built, and he can’t see where the money went. Ndivuho Mafela is the Head: Stakeholder Relations, Marketing and Communications at the National Lotteries Commission. He confirmed that the NLC had approved the R27.5 million budget for the project, but says that they stopped a final payment when they were notified of the pending civil and criminal cases.

Sound Up Ndivuho
Devi: How much money was paid out to Denzhe Primary Care?

Ndivuho: The money that was paid out to Denzhe Primary Care will be about R19 million.

Link Devi
This report, written by an independent specialist, says in total, no more than R4.8 million was spent at the rehab.

Voice
We wanted to know how Lesley Ramulifho had spent the money, but he declined our offer of an on-camera interview for this broadcast and he has to date not sent us detailed answers to our written questions. Meanwhile our documents raise serious questions about the NLC’s proactive funding mechanism, signed off by NLC commissioner Thabang Mampane in the Denzhe case. The very same proactive funding that allowed the fast tracking of the Denzhe grant.

Sound Up Ndivuho
Ndivuho: It can take us up to three months to make a grant or to make a decision on the grant, so the question was what happens if there have been emergencies? So that’s where this whole system of proactive funding was initiated.

Voice
So why would the Denzhe deal qualify as Pro Active funding?

Devi: Where was the emergency factor there?

Ndivuho: There might not be a necessary emergency now, but if you look at it you have got a scourge of drug use, right?

Voice:
The Organisation Undoing Tax Abuse, OUTA, is investigating alleged abuses of proactive funding by the NLC. Dominique Msibi is their Special Projects manager.

Sound Up Dominique
There’s hardly an application if you can call it that, because they go to the NGO and offer the funding. It is definitely not your traditional, regular, we are used to application process.

Voice
According to our sources, family members of the NLC’s Chief Operating Officer Phillemon Letwaba, who’s signature is also on the grant approvals, stood to score from the deal.

Link Devi
This is the construction contract entered into between Denzhe and Upbrand Properties. It raises questions about Lesley Ramulifho’s ties to the Lotteries Commission because in October 2016 when this was signed, the sole director of Upbrand Properties was Johannes Kgomotso Letwaba, the brother of the NLC’s COO Phillemon Letwaba.

Voice
The total value of the construction side of the project was R15 million.

Sound Up Ndivuho
Devi: So, the word on the street is that Johannes Letwaba, yes you know where I’m going with this, is Phillemon Letwaba your COO’s brother. Are you aware of that?

Ndivuho: Ja I’m aware of that

Devi: Is that true?

Ndivuho: Yes, it’s true.

Devi: Hah

Ndivuho: Yes

Devi: Wait, so your COO Phillemon Letwaba, his brother was given the R15million contract to do construction on this project?

Ndivuho: The issue that you are raising, it has been raised several times of the conflict of interest in the matter with regards to our COO. And what has happened there has been an investigation that was conducted…

Devi: Ja

Ndivuho: which went to the board level, and then the report as well as usual goes to sit with the minister.

Voice
The board found that Phillemon Letwaba had declared the conflict of interest, but that’s not the end of the saga.

Link Devi
We also discovered hundreds of thousands paid out of Denzhe’s account to a restaurant chain - not for take-out, but allegedly for franchise payments.

Voice
Two payments totalling R535 240 of the NLC funds that Denzhe received, allegedly went towards the partial payments of two restaurants that Lesley Ramulifho now owns.

Sound Up Ndivuho
Ndivuho: Yes the NLC are quite aware of that because Denzhe wrote a report that there had been loans that had been taken, these are the loan agreements, and from where we sit, according to the reports that we have been given, the money has since been paid off, back.

Devi: You guys couldn’t have been happy when you saw that?

Ndivuho: Surely, we are not because it breaches the grant agreement but those are the things that we are investigating. And then while we were, it’s quite drama, while we were busy with that, trying to mediate this side and do that then there are court cases, which really tie our hands.

Voice
But it seems that despite all the controversy, Lesley Ramulifho is beyond reproach at the NLC.

Link Devi
According to other leaked documents, the Denzhe Primary Care deal was not the only time Lesley Ramulifho received money from the NLC. He can be linked to other grants totalling millions, but here’s the kicker. He received the funds despite the NLC knowing there were issues with the rehab project.

Voice
In April last year, Lesley Ramulifho and one of his other NPO’s called I am made 4 God’s Glory, was approved for yet another grant totaling R11 375 000 for sports and recreation facilities.

Sound Up Ndivuho
Devi: Despite all this drama here, which you knew about, while you’re waiting for an outcome at the court, you give him another project.

Ndivuho: We gave a different organisation another project.

Devi: Which he’s associated with that NPO. He’s the chairman.

Ndivuho: They are different proposals, talking about totally different things. Why should I assess a totally different sports centre based on the rehabilitation centre? Because that’s totally different in different areas.

Voice
Meanwhile Krige says he’s eagerly awaiting his day in court.

Sound Up Ado
I live by what I preach, you shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free. And the public need to know the truth of what went down here.

Sound Up Ado Ado: Now lo and behold, R5 million standing there. Devi: What’s that? Ado: That’s a sport centre. Devi: No man. Ado: Ja that’s a sport Centre, R5million rand sports Centre. All that he did there was put on a new roof. Voice And he says what currently passes for the sports centre was an existing building that used to be his lapa. Sound Up Ado This was our table; you can see it’s old. Ok, this used to be my Lapa and the equipment that you see in here I promise you is all my old equipment. Voice According to Krige the building shown as the sports centre in the architectural drawings does in fact not exist on site, Link Devi I need your help here. I need you to use your imagination and picture a R5 million sports Centre, right here, with all the bells and whistles. Can you picture it? Neither can I. Voice A new classroom, two blocks of living quarters and the auditorium have been finished but Krige says they’re shoddily built, and he can’t see where the money went. Ndivuho Mafela is the Head: Stakeholder Relations, Marketing and Communications at the National Lotteries Commission. He confirmed that the NLC had approved the R27.5 million budget for the project, but says that they stopped a final payment when they were notified of the pending civil and criminal cases. Sound Up Ndivuho Devi: How much money was paid out to Denzhe Primary Care? Ndivuho: The money that was paid out to Denzhe Primary Care will be about R19 million. Link Devi This report, written by an independent specialist, says in total, no more than R4.8 million was spent at the rehab. Voice We wanted to know how Lesley Ramulifho had spent the money, but he declined our offer of an on-camera interview for this broadcast and he has to date not sent us detailed answers to our written questions. Meanwhile our documents raise serious questions about the NLC’s proactive funding mechanism, signed off by NLC commissioner Thabang Mampane in the Denzhe case. The very same proactive funding that allowed the fast tracking of the Denzhe grant. Sound Up Ndivuho Ndivuho: It can take us up to three months to make a grant or to make a decision on the grant, so the question was what happens if there have been emergencies? So that’s where this whole system of proactive funding was initiated. Voice So why would the Denzhe deal qualify as Pro Active funding? Devi: Where was the emergency factor there? Ndivuho: There might not be a necessary emergency now, but if you look at it you have got a scourge of drug use, right? Voice: The Organisation Undoing Tax Abuse, OUTA, is investigating alleged abuses of proactive funding by the NLC. Dominique Msibi is their Special Projects manager. Sound Up Dominique There’s hardly an application if you can call it that, because they go to the NGO and offer the funding. It is definitely not your traditional, regular, we are used to application process. Voice According to our sources, family members of the NLC’s Chief Operating Officer Phillemon Letwaba, who’s signature is also on the grant approvals, stood to score from the deal. Link Devi This is the construction contract entered into between Denzhe and Upbrand Properties. It raises questions about Lesley Ramulifho’s ties to the Lotteries Commission because in October 2016 when this was signed, the sole director of Upbrand Properties was Johannes Kgomotso Letwaba, the brother of the NLC’s COO Phillemon Letwaba. Voice The total value of the construction side of the project was R15 million. Sound Up Ndivuho Devi: So, the word on the street is that Johannes Letwaba, yes you know where I’m going with this, is Phillemon Letwaba your COO’s brother. Are you aware of that? Ndivuho: Ja I’m aware of that Devi: Is that true? Ndivuho: Yes, it’s true. Devi: Hah Ndivuho: Yes Devi: Wait, so your COO Phillemon Letwaba, his brother was given the R15million contract to do construction on this project? Ndivuho: The issue that you are raising, it has been raised several times of the conflict of interest in the matter with regards to our COO. And what has happened there has been an investigation that was conducted… Devi: Ja Ndivuho: which went to the board level, and then the report as well as usual goes to sit with the minister. Voice The board found that Phillemon Letwaba had declared the conflict of interest, but that’s not the end of the saga. Link Devi We also discovered hundreds of thousands paid out of Denzhe’s account to a restaurant chain - not for take-out, but allegedly for franchise payments. Voice Two payments totalling R535 240 of the NLC funds that Denzhe received, allegedly went towards the partial payments of two restaurants that Lesley Ramulifho now owns. Sound Up Ndivuho Ndivuho: Yes the NLC are quite aware of that because Denzhe wrote a report that there had been loans that had been taken, these are the loan agreements, and from where we sit, according to the reports that we have been given, the money has since been paid off, back. Devi: You guys couldn’t have been happy when you saw that? Ndivuho: Surely, we are not because it breaches the grant agreement but those are the things that we are investigating. And then while we were, it’s quite drama, while we were busy with that, trying to mediate this side and do that then there are court cases, which really tie our hands. Voice But it seems that despite all the controversy, Lesley Ramulifho is beyond reproach at the NLC. Link Devi According to other leaked documents, the Denzhe Primary Care deal was not the only time Lesley Ramulifho received money from the NLC. He can be linked to other grants totalling millions, but here’s the kicker. He received the funds despite the NLC knowing there were issues with the rehab project. Voice In April last year, Lesley Ramulifho and one of his other NPO’s called I am made 4 God’s Glory, was approved for yet another grant totaling R11 375 000 for sports and recreation facilities. Sound Up Ndivuho Devi: Despite all this drama here, which you knew about, while you’re waiting for an outcome at the court, you give him another project. Ndivuho: We gave a different organisation another project. Devi: Which he’s associated with that NPO. He’s the chairman. Ndivuho: They are different proposals, talking about totally different things. Why should I assess a totally different sports centre based on the rehabilitation centre? Because that’s totally different in different areas. Voice Meanwhile Krige says he’s eagerly awaiting his day in court. Sound Up Ado I live by what I preach, you shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free. And the public need to know the truth of what went down here.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We investigate an illusive Pretoria based lawyer and find out how he managed to receive millions from the National Lotteries Commission for supposed charitable projects that never materialised.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Attorney, Lesley Ramulifh, allegedly received a total of R27.5 million rand from the NLC to refurbish an existing NPO and drug rehabilitation centre in Pretoria. But soon after construction started, the owner of the rehab, Ado Krige, started questioning Lesley on construction delays etc, as well as the fact that contrary to their agreement Lesley wanted Ado to sell the rehab to him. Since then construction (according to an independent report the value of work done only totals R4 million) has stopped. Ado has taken his case to the NLC who seem unwilling to do anything about the situation. Lesley received the R27.5 million by calling himself a director of an NPO called Denzhe Primary Care. We can prove that at least some of the money Denzhe received, about half a million rand, went towards purchasing two Ocean Basket franchises. We can also prove that the construction company Lesley appointed to do the R15 million refurbishment of the rehab, Upbrand Properties was registered in January 2016 with Johannes Kgomotso Letwaba, the older brother of the NLC’s COO, Phillemon Letwaba, as the sole director.
metadata.Summary: Except for the Denzhe deal, we can also link Lesley to 3 other NPO's, Zibsifusion, I am made 4 God's glory, and Dinosys, which received R31 million from the NLC, for projects that don't seem to have materialised. Lesley is the chairperson of I am made 4 God's Glory, while the other two are chaired by people who work for Lesley's law firm Ramulifho Inc.
metadata.Further information: Although the Denzhe story has been reported by Ground Up and then covered in the Citizen, the story has received very little traction. We have documentary proof of all the funds received and grant allocations made to Ramulifho and his associates. It is plain to see at Ado's rehab that the work, according to the grant allocation, has not been done. There is a clear conflict of interest in the NLC's COO and the sole director of the construction company. The only images we have available of Ramulifho is about 25 instagram posts by his girlfriend Melanie, which show the couple's jetsetting lifestyle in the past two years with trips to Bali, Isreal, Qatar etc and flying first class. We have internal NLC docs showing the funding of R27.5 mil was approved and paid, and that the NLC did a final site visit to declare the project was completed according to spec. (We cannot show these because source would be compromised). While Ramulifho needs to answer the allegations against him, the real problem is the NLC releasing funds to him without any sort of due diligence. The NLC needs to be held to account, but in the articles published they have seemed to come off lightly.
